item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox open up a three-game series against AL East rival Tampa Bay Rays on Friday, September 18, at Tropicana Field.
Ranger Suarez will get the ball for Boston tonight. After that, the pitching plans are unclear. The Red Sox have listed TBDs for their starting pitcher spot on Saturday and Sunday, per Tim Healey of the Boston Globe. Payton Tolle and Patrick Sandoval were lined up to start this weekend, but that is now in doubt.
Probable pitchers for Red Sox-Rays this weekend…
* Friday: Ranger Suarez vs. Ian Seymour* Saturday: TBD vs. Freddy Peralta* Sunday: TBD vs. Griffin Jax
Saturday would be Payton Tolle's day, if the Red Sox stay on turn. We'll see how they handle it.
— Tim Healey (@timbhealey) September 17, 2026
Tolle has already zoomed past his previous career high in innings as a pro. The lefty tossed 108 frames between the minors and majors in 2025. Tolle has thrown 158 innings across both levels this season.
Boston Red Sox May Skip Payton Tolle Against the Tampa Bay Rays
Tolle has been a fixture in Boston's rotation for much of the season. He's posted a 3.03 ERA across 25 starts with the big-league club. The young lefty opened the season in the minors, but was promoted to the majors in April. Tolle has solidified a pitching staff that has dealt with injuries and underperformance at times in 2026.
While he won't win AL Rookie of the Year, Tolle has put together a solid case. He's right up there with Cleveland Guardians left-hander Parker Messick as the top rookie starter in the American League. Kevin McGonigle of the Detroit Tigers and Munetaka Murakami of the Chicago White Sox are the betting favorites, but Tolle and Messick will receive some down-ballot votes.
Tolle struggled to a 6.06 ERA in his first taste of the big leagues last year. He missed bats at a decent 25.7% clip, but notched a 10.8% walk rate. The lefty has improved in both departments this season. Tolle pushed his strikeout rate to 28.9% and trimmed his walk rate to 6.6% in his first full campaign as a major league starter.
Red Sox Lining Up Postseason Rotation
Moving Tolle's next start could be an effort to align the playoff rotation. The pitching staff will likely be headlined by Sonny Gray, but the second and third slots are up for grabs. Suarez has a solid case to pitch the second game of the Wild Card round. The gig could also go to Tolle.
Sandoval and Jake Bennett are likely looking at long relief roles in the first round of the playoffs. Both have had decent stretches this season, but faded recently. Bennett has permitted a dozen runs in three September starts. Sandoval has a 7.82 ERA this month.
Brayan Bello is the question mark among the unit. He's struggled as a starter and been tremendous out of the bullpen. Bello could operate in tandem with one of Boston's many left-handed starters.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox made one of the very best moves in baseball for the 2026 season, despite the fact that some fans didn't initially believe in the deal.
While searching for a No. 2 starter last offseason, Boston turned to the St. Louis Cardinals and swung a deal for three-time All-Star Sonny Gray. With the Red Sox searching for another elite starter, some wondered if Gray was better suited for a mid-to-back of the rotation spot, rather than the No. 2 spot for a club with World Series aspirations. He has more than delivered and has been Boston's best starter all season. Gray's going to get Cy Young Award votes and Boston should do what it can to try to keep him in town beyond the 2026 season. If he plays, he'll cost a pretty penny. MassLive.com's Chris Cotillo reported that some in the industry believe Gray will get a deal in the range of three years and $75 million — or more — if he continues his career.
"As a free agent, Gray’s renaissance season may position him to receive a lucrative deal that some in the industry expect to match or exceed the three-year, $75 million deal the Rangers gave to Nathan Eovaldi two winters ago," Cotillo wrote. "Interestingly, though, Gray has not committed to pitching again in 2027. In a recent interview with The Boston Globe, Gray said he would retire 'in a heartbeat' if his family signaled that he was wanted back home year-round, even if that meant retiring after the end of this year."
The Red Sox Should Do Everything To Keep Sonny Gray
That's actually also the same deal that the Cardinals gave Gray before the 2024 season as well. He inked a three-year, $75 million pact that he's currently in the final year of. After the season, Gray has a $30 million mutual option for the 2027 season with a $10 million buyout. If Boston picks up its end of the buyout and Gray opts out, then the buyout would be forfeited.
Gray has pitched well enough in a Red Sox uniform to get paid again — if he keeps pitching. So far this season, he has a 17-5 record, 2.76 ERA and 4.0 wins above replacement in 156 2/3 innings pitched. When it comes to Gray, his age stands out at 36 years old. But it hasn't stopped him yet. The price of pitching has gone up in a big way. A deal with a $25 million annual value, as Cotillo pointed out, would be in the range of guys like Michael King, Sean Manaea, and Eovaldi. It would be just above guys like Aaron Nola, Seth Lugo, Robbie Ray and Luis Severino. Gray has been better than all of these guys so far this season.
When it comes to the Red Sox, there isn't as much pitching depth down in the minors as there once was. Over the last year, Boston has traded guys like Hunter Dobbins, Richard Fitts, Brandon Clarke, Anthony Eyanson and Kyson Witherspoon, among others. Plus, Connelly Early was traded as well.
Garrett Crochet, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suárez, and Jake Bennett are locks for the 2027 rotation. Johan Oviedo is someone who could play a role. Tanner Houck is another guy who could as well. We've seen all season how impactful injuries are to the rotation. You never have enough arms. A dependable veteran like Gray for the next few years should be a necessity. It's no guarantee that he pitches beyond the 2026 season, but if he does, it should be in a Boston uniform.

Good morning! Last night, Jake Bennett was unable to hold the Rangers in check during the team's 7-3 loss in Texas. Some of his numbers look good (seven strikeouts against just one walk), but he also surrendered eight hits in just 4.2 innings, which did in his evening.
With just ten games left in the season, the question now becomes how should the Sox use Bennett going forward? With some combination of Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle and Ranger Suarez likely to get lined up in a best of three Wild Card Series, do you just hold Bennett on the sidelines and hope he gets to come back into the fold as a fourth starter in the ALDS or even ALCS? Or do you start transitioning him to some sort of relief role?
It's a bit of an awkward moment for Bennett. He's been getting knocked around during his last two outings while Suarez is seemingly getting locked in. It almost certainly cuts him out of the Wild Card rotation, and if the Sox get some combination of Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck and Tyron Guerrero back to add to Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock and Erik Miller in the bullpen, Bennett largely gets squeezed out of relevance.
So how do you want him used? Do those six shutout innings Bennett threw against the Yankees back on August 29th make you want the Sox to find a role for him if they play New York? Do you think he's just a young pitcher who looks out of gas and want to hide him until the team needs a fourth starter?
Use this space to talk about Bennett and the rest of the difficult upcoming pitching staff decisions, and, as always, be good to one another.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox probably won't get a full sense of their 2026 trade deadline performance this season, despite the positive injury updates on Curtis Mead. The former Washington National will hit off a tee in the coming days — his first offensive progress since he succumbed to a wrist injury during his Red Sox debut — but there's a good chance he doesn't progress fast enough to return this year.
On the other hand, the Nationals will soon get a look at their return from the trade, Connelly Early. The young lefty was on the injured list with elbow inflammation when the Nats traded for him on July 26. He's recently taken some major steps in his rehab.
Washington on September 13 sent Early on a rehab assignment. In one inning with the Triple-A Rochester Red Wings, he allowed three runs on two hits and two walks with two strikeouts.
Nationals President of Baseball Operations (and former Red Sox Assistant General Manager) Paul Toboni confirmed on "The Sports Junkies" show on 106.7 The Fan that Early will make another rehab appearance on September 20 before he makes his DC debut on September 26 against the New York Mets. The season ends on September 28, so Washington will get a look at Early in the major leagues just in time.
Nationals confirm former Red Sox pitcher Connelly Early will make first big league start since trade on September 26
The Nationals were eliminated from playoff contention over the weekend, which could be one reason they're letting Early start. It's already been over two months since the rookie last pitched, but there's no stakes on getting a preview of Early's talent.
Early posted a 3.44 ERA, 1.25 WHIP, 93 strikeouts and 34 walks over 91.2 innings with the Red Sox this season. Washington's rotation hasn't looked sharp lately, despite Cade Cavalli's utter dominance since he faced the Red Sox on June 30 (2.27 ERA, 0.90 WHIP, 112 strikeouts over his last 15 games). Early will be an upgrade over Jake Irvin (5.51 ERA in 96.1 innings) or rookie Jackson Kent (6.40 ERA in 32.1 innings), who has only pitched a tiny sample size of innings, but they haven't been good.
The Red Sox's rotation could use another arm given Patrick Sandoval and Jake Bennett's recent struggles, but holding onto Early wouldn't have done much for them given his long IL stint during the playoff race. Boston dealt from a position of depth to acquire Mead and it deserves credit for doing so despite the unfortunate circumstances that led to his placement on the IL.
Just in the nick of time, the Nationals will get to see what Early can do on the mound before the season ends. The Red Sox may not get so lucky with Mead, even though their season will continue into October.

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON -- Despite getting an early two-run homer from Willson Contreras and taking advantage of a handful of Rangers miscues, the Red Sox couldn’t hold off Texas in a 7-3 loss on Wednesday at Globe Life Field.
The loss, however, didn’t change Boston's position in the postseason race, as the club remained in the second AL Wild Card spot and maintained its five-game cushion over the White Sox after Chicago lost to the Guardians earlier Wednesday.
Roman Anthony opened the game with a four-pitch walk. After Jahmai Jones flied out, Wilyer Abreu grounded into a forceout but beat the relay throw to first to avoid the double play and keep the inning alive for Contreras.
“Those are important details,” Contreras said in Spanish. “They don’t go unnoticed because they matter a lot in this game.”
With the postseason nearing, those -- along with having success with ABS challenges -- are the types of details Contreras was glad to see the Red Sox execute, especially with close games likely to become more common down the stretch. Boston had six successful challenges Wednesday night, and catcher Adley Rutschman improved to 19-for-27 on ABS challenges since joining the Red Sox.
Contreras entered the night batting .563 in his career against Rangers starter MacKenzie Gore, and helped set up his two-run homer with an early ABS challenge on a called strike that missed the bottom of the zone. After the call was overturned, Contreras took advantage when Gore left an 87 mph slider over the middle of the plate, sending it out to left-center field for his 27th homer of the season and an early 2-0 Red Sox lead.
“Honestly, I really liked that challenge, because I was sure it was a little bit under,” Contreras said. “And after that, I had the opportunity to get a pitch a little bit higher and connect for a home run.”
Contreras’ familiarity with Gore has also helped. The two faced each other frequently when Gore was with the Nationals and Contreras played for the Cubs and Cardinals.
“I know him well and I know that he always makes one or two errors in a game, so I am always trying to be ready for that error, like today,” Contreras said. “I wasn’t looking for that pitch, I was just looking for him to miss his spot in the middle.”
It was Contreras’ 27th homer of the season and his first since Aug. 21 against the Giants.
Texas eventually erased that advantage, pulling even at 2 in the fourth, but the Rangers helped Boston regain the lead an inning later.
Caleb Durbin drew Boston’s third walk of the night against Gore to begin the fifth. Trevor Story then sent a liner toward third baseman Josh Jung, who was unable to make a play. Durbin immediately recognized the opportunity, rounding second and advancing to third as Jung was slow to get the ball back into the infield.
The sequence ended Gore’s night and brought right-hander Jakob Junis out of the Rangers' bullpen. As Junis came set to face pinch-hitter Mickey Gasper, the ball slipped out of his glove for a balk, allowing Durbin to score and put the Red Sox back in front.
“We're going through it a little bit,” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “We didn't create a ton of opportunities. Obviously, Willson with a big swing to give us the lead, and only a couple other chances. ... That's it. So really, [getting] three runs on the board with only three hits was good in that sense. But just not creating a ton of opportunities for ourselves today.”
The 3-2 lead was short-lived, as Texas answered in the bottom half of the fifth to tie the game again.
Boston’s starter, Jake Bennett, worked through a 26-pitch first inning, limiting Texas to one run despite allowing two doubles and a single, before giving up another run in the fourth.
The game turned in the seventh, when reliever Erik Miller allowed three runs on two hits. Texas added another run in the eighth off Raymond Burgos.
“As a team, I think we're doing the best we can to capitalize on every chance we have,” Contreras said. “We battle. We come here with the right mindset. We work hard. We work on details that we need to get better on.
“And sometimes it doesn't matter how hard you work. Sometimes the results are not gonna come. But you have to build off that. You have to take those types of games personal and get better for tomorrow.”

The regular season is rapidly coming to an end, and the Boston Red Sox still don't have ace pitcher Garrett Crochet back. That could be changing soon, though.
It had previously been reported that Crochet was set to return for the first round of the playoffs. Now, Chris Cotillo of MassLive noted in a report that the Red Sox may be pushing to have Crochet pitch in the regular season. This would act as a kind of rehab outing.
"The comebacks of potential October contributors like Tanner Houck, Garrett Crochet, Johan Oviedo and others might also be aided by the fact the Red Sox might have a week (or more) to set up for the postseason," Cotillo wrote. "It's not out of the question that the club has someone like Crochet pitch in one of the final regular season games of the year in what's effectively a rehab outing at the major league level in a game that matters little in the standings."
After finishing second in AL Cy Young voting in 2025, 2026 has been a major disappointment for Crochet. He has a 6.30 ERA and hasn't pitched since April 29th, when he originally hit the IL with left shoulder inflammation. He would later also be diagnosed with a lat strain.
When Crochet does return, it won't be in the rotation. He doesn't have time to build up to that. Instead, the Red Sox are going to be using him out of the bullpen. he
Boston Red Sox Ace Garrett Crochet Doesn't Have Time for a Rehab
The reality for Garrett Crochet is that time is running out for a rehab assignment, and he likely won't have time to make one. That's why the Red Sox would likely want to bring him back before a playoff series.
Regardless of if that chance to come back before the postseason happens, however, Crochet is confident in himself.
"Someone brought it up the other day. They were like, isn't that crazy? I'm like, not really," Crochet said on Monday. "I mean, not [to be all] me, me, me, me, but I've done crazy things before. I'm not Joe Schmoe. I've done impressive things. I think that that would be a big ask for some people, but I don't think it's a crazy ask for me."
This isn't entirely new territory for Crochet. In 2020, the Chicago White Sox added him to their postseason roster when he had limited time in live action due to the pandemic and coming out of college. He pitched well in that brief opportunity, throwing 0.2 innings with 2 strikeouts.
The Red Sox Postseason Rotation is Up for Debate
Heading into the postseason, pitching is a strength for the Red Sox. Even with injuries, that much has become obvious. Still, questions remain about the actual rotation in the postseason.
Sonny Gray and Payton Tolle will make starts in a three-game series. That's not up for debate. There is debate about which of the two gets Game One. Then, Game Three is going to be between Ranger Suarez and Jake Bennett. The lean there is certainly for the well-paid Suarez, who is a veteran with postseason success. However, stranger things have happened.
Starters who could be coming back from injury, including Houck and Crochet, are going to be seen as relievers. That's presumably how the Red Sox will also continue to use Brayan Bello and Patrick Sandoval.

The limp to October goes on for the Boston Red Sox, who blew an early 2-0 lead Wednesday night, and dropped the series in Texas with a 7-3 loss that improved the Rangers to 76-76.
Boston batters managed just three hits, their runs coming via Willson Contreras’ first-inning two-run homer and Caleb Durbin scoring on a balk in the fifth.
Early on, it looked like both starting pitchers were not going to last long.
Rangers lefty MacKenzie Gore began Wednesday’s game with a four-pitch walk, three of which were nowhere near the zone, to Red Sox leadoff man Roman Anthony, and gave up Contreras’ team-leading 27th homer.
Sox rookie southpaw Jake Bennett labored through a 26-pitch bottom of the first in which he faced six batters and gave up a run.
But after a second-inning delay in which it seemed like Gore was about to depart, he completed four innings. Bennett went 4 2/3. Both starters allowed three earned runs, though Gore only yielded two hits to Bennett’s eight.
“Overall, not horrible,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters of Bennett. “The first inning they were able to make him throw some pitches, so the pitches stacked up on him. But at the end of the day, he left with the lead, was competitive. … Usually you’re accustomed to see him pitching deeper, but they were pesky with their at-bats, fouled a lot of stuff off, and drove the count up.”
The Red Sox retook the lead on Jakob Junis’ fifth-inning balk. It evaporated for good one pitch into Greg Weissert’s appearance when he took over for Bennett in the bottom of the inning.
Erik Miller’s three-run blowup seventh inning was the unnecessary coup de grâce for a Red Sox team struggling to so much as collect a hit, much less score a run. But it marked Miller’s worst outing of the season, with Boston or San Francisco, and his third time allowing runs in his last six appearances.
“Just not doing what I’ve been doing well, just not getting ahead of guys, falling behind counts, getting into hitters counts,” a subdued Miller told reporters postgame. “I mean, doesn’t really matter how good your stuff is; guy knows what’s coming, it usually doesn’t end as well.”
“Just kind of working through some stuff right now,” Miller continued. “There’s some stuff (I’m) trying to clean up a little bit on the mechanical side. … At some point throughout the year, stuff crops up. And I’d been doing really well, and some bad habits kind of fallen back into. So yeah, just got to work through it, kind of get back to what I was doing, and go from there.”
2018 World Series hero Nathan Eovaldi closed out the win with four shutout innings against his former team. It marked the veteran righty’s first relief appearance since 2020: Game 4 of the 2021 ALCS with the Red Sox.
To add insult to the injury of Boston’s decision not to re-sign Eovaldi following the 2022 season, his 46 wins since 2023 are tied for second-most among all American League pitchers in that span.
Trevor Story’s infield single in the fifth and Nick Sogard’s pinch-hit single in the sixth comprised the rest of Boston’s hits. The lineup managed three walks and struck out three times in the contest. They were 0 for 7 with runners in scoring position, and left three men on base.
“Yeah, we’re going through it a little bit,” Tracy said of his lineup. “We didn’t have a ton, we didn’t create a ton of opportunities.”
Game highlights were few and far between for the Red Sox. The short list included the usual elite defense from right fielder Wilyer Abreu, who is all but guaranteed to win his third consecutive Gold Glove Award, and continued displays of ABS expertise by new catcher Adley Rutschman, who went 3 for 3 in challenges.
The Red Sox have lost five of their last seven games since their five-game win streak. They are 7-7 in September, 10-11 in their last 20 games, and 82-70 overall.
Their magic number to clinch a postseason spot is five. But there is little magic lately.

The Boston Red are losers of four games out of their last six after dropping Tuesday's 4-2 decision to the Texas Rangers.
As they push to clinch a playoff spot, the Red Sox send rookie left-hander Jake Bennett (9-7, 3.69, 83 K) to the mound in the middle contest of the three game series in Texas.
Just hours before first pitch, the Red Sox announced a decision on their left-swinging outfielder Jarren Duran.
Duran is sitting out again Wednesday as the Boston Red Sox face Texas Rangers left-hander MacKenzie Gore, extending a pattern now seven starts deep. The decision appears to be strictly a platoon move by interim manager Chad Tracy. There have been no reports that Duran is injured.
In fact, Boston has now benched its left-handed-hitting outfielder against every left-handed starter he has faced since Aug. 8, a stretch that raises concerns about how Duran fits into next season's outfield picture, and for the likely American League wild-card series matchup.
In that three-game series, the Red Sox appear certain to face at least one left-hander, possibly two, in Yankees starters Max Fried and Carlos Rodón.

Duran's absence from the lineup against lefties has stretched to seven straight starts without facing a southpaw, dating back to his last look at left-handed pitching on Aug. 8, according to RotoWire. He sat again Sunday against Kansas City and was used only as a pinch-hitter, a role he has filled repeatedly this month.
There is no reported health issue behind Tracy's decision. Duran started Tuesday against right-hander Jacob deGrom, playing center field and batting seventh, and remains fully active on Boston's roster.
Duran is slashing .204/.261/.361 with 20 home runs across 141 games this season, and his OPS against left-handed pitching sits at .641, actually higher than his .616 mark against right-handers, according to FanGraphs. Boston has kept sitting him against lefties anyway.

Boston opened the year with four outfielders competing for time, but an early injury to Roman Anthony briefly opened the picture before Duran struggled through a rough first half, batting .194 over his first 87 games. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox haven't officially clinched a postseason spot, but all signs point toward a Wild Card Series rematch at Yankee Stadium.
Pitching depth was a problem for the Red Sox in last year's playoff meeting with the Yankees. Their ace Garrett Crochet propelled them to victory in Game 1, but Brayan Bello and an inexperienced Connelly Early couldn't get the job done in Games 2 and 3.
This time, Boston's pitching will be a strength. Veteran right-hander Sonny Gray, rookie southpaw Payton Tolle, and veteran lefty Ranger Suarez can go toe-to-toe with most clubs' 1-through-3. The question is, what's the optimal order to put them in for the three-game Wild Card Series?
It's a good problem to have, and there's really no wrong answer. That said, here's our ideal Wild Card Series rotation for Boston as it looks to avenge last year's crushing defeat:
Justin Leger
Game 1: Sonny Gray
Gray isn't the "sexy" pick. That would be the mustached man I have starting Game 2.
But in what's sure to be an electrifying environment at Yankee Stadium, I want a dependable veteran on the mound to begin the series. I want Mr. Consistency.
All season long, Gray has fit that description.
Gray has a 17-5 record (tied for MLB lead in wins) with a 2.76 ERA through 27 starts. Since Crochet went down with an early-season injury, the 36-year-old has stepped up as the Red Sox' de facto ace with 18 quality starts (tied for seventh in MLB).
Unlike Tolle, Gray has plenty of experience pitching at Yankee Stadium. He's had his fair share of rough starts there throughout his 14-year career, especially during his brief stint with New York, but he was solid there earlier this season with three earned runs across 6.1 innings pitched in a 5-3 victory. In his other start against the Yankees at Fenway Park, he took a no-hitter into the eighth inning.
It'll be an uphill battle for the Red Sox regardless of who's on the mound, because Cy Young frontrunner Cam Schlittler will be poised to shut down Boston's bats yet again. Still, Gray can be counted on to give the Sox a chance to win, and if they lose, they'll have great options to lean on in Games 2 and 3.
Game 2: Payton Tolle
If Tolle is named the Red Sox' Game 1 starter, I won't complain. I'd be slightly concerned that his 0.1 IP in last year's Wild Card Series marks his only experience pitching at Yankee Stadium, but that isn't worth panicking about. He seems built for the bright lights.
Tolle looked sharp in both of his starts against the Yankees at Fenway this season. During his first outing in April, the 23-year-old allowed just one run on three hits across six innings. In his second start against them in June, he carried a perfect game into the sixth inning, finishing with no runs and just one hit allowed over seven innings pitched.
Those were two of many outings this season in which Tolle has looked like an ace. He'll have to perform like one throughout Boston's postseason run, and if he gets the ball in Game 2, he might be counted on to keep Boston's season alive.
Game 3: Ranger Suarez
If it comes down to a do-or-die Game 3, I feel great about Ranger Suarez taking the mound. The 31-year-old veteran has the postseason pedigree with an impressive 1.48 ERA in 11 career appearances (eight starts) with the Philadelphia Phillies.
Suarez endured a second-half slump but has looked more like himself in his last two outings. After tossing seven shutout innings against the Baltimore Orioles on Sept. 4, he allowed just one run across seven innings while striking out eight Kansas City Royals hitters on Saturday. This is the version of Suarez the Red Sox expected to get when they signed him to a five-year, $130 million contract in the offseason.
If Suarez struggles, the Red Sox will have the luxury of an elite bullpen to lean on. Brayan Bello has been an excellent bulk option since reverting to a relief role. Jake Bennett could be a legitimate weapon out of the 'pen as well, along with Crochet if he returns in time from his injury.
Mitchael Hurley
Game 1: Payton Tolle
I'm not opposed to statistics influencing baseball decisions. I rely on statistics more than I should.
But in this case, I don't think they matter. If you've watched the Red Sox this year, it could not be more clear that Payton Tolle is very much the heart and soul of this team. And the idea of sending him out onto the mound at Yankee Stadium with the whole baseball world watching just feels like the obvious choice.
If the Red Sox are going to win a series like this one, they're going to need to be the team with more energy. Nobody would bring more juice to the mound than Tolle. If he can step onto the field on a rainy Sunday four hours after first pitch was scheduled and instantly deliver an immaculate inning in the first, it's frightening to think what type of energy he can bring to a Game 1 start.
The Yankees have struggled against him this year, but even if they hadn't, I've gotta send Tolle to the mound for Game 1.
Game 2: Sonny Gray
In another year, in another circumstance, the 36-year-old Sonny Gray would be in line to win his first career Cy Young Award.
Of course, Cam Schlittler, the Yankees' presumed Game 1 starter, has wrecked any and all Cy Young debate with his sterling season in New York. Still, Gray is having one of the best seasons of his 14-year career, and he has to pitch in this series.
He did allow a pair of homers in his lone start at Yankee Stadium this season, and he's given up 22 homers in 23 appearances there in his career. With the short porch looming and the crowd always looking to erupt, that would be my concern.
But Gray's been great all year, he's been great down the stretch, and the Red Sox will ensure that he's properly rested for this one.
Game 3: Ranger Suarez
Would it look bad if the Red Sox potentially lost the series in two games and never sent Ranger Suarez and his 1.48 postseason ERA to the mound? It sure would.
But given the years that Tolle and Gray have had, I think the Red Sox could live with it.
There is some concern that he got rocked in the Bronx on Aug. 30 (six earned runs in 5.1 innings), but he also allowed one run in six innings in his first start at Yankee Stadium earlier in the season.
Considering the Red Sox had to send rookie Connelly Early out there in Game 3 a year ago to make his fifth career start, the team is clearly in a much better position if another Game 3 awaits them in the Bronx.

Alex Cora said Braiden Ward would be a factor in October.
The Boston Red Sox outfield depth took a major hit ahead of last Friday’s series opener against the Kansas City Royals as the team placed Eli White on the 10-day injured list with a right foot ligament injury, with no timetable for his return. The 32-year-old outfielder not only filled in admirably for the injured Ceddanne Rafaela, but was also slated to play an important role on the postseason roster as the fourth outfielder and pinch runner off the bench. With White now unlikely to return before the postseason, could the Red Sox turn to spring-training standout Braiden Ward to fill the role?
About Ward
The Red Sox acquired Ward in an offseason deal with the Colorado Rockies in exchange for left-handed reliever Brennan Bernardino. The 27-year-old outfielder became one of the biggest storylines of Red Sox spring training, seeing ample playing time as many of Boston's outfield options, including Roman Anthony, Wilyer Abreu and Rafaela, represented their countries in the World Baseball Classic. In 27 Grapefruit League games, Ward hit .378/.509/.444/.953 while stealing 19 bases, setting a single-season spring training record. Ward's dynamic speed caught the eye of now-former manager Alex Cora, who told reporters on several occasions that the 27-year-old would be a factor come October.
After missing the team's opening-day roster amid an already crowded outfield, Ward spent the entire 2026 season in Triple-A Worcester. In 107 games with the WooSox, Ward hit just .238/.356/.355/.711 but set a record for most stolen bases in a single season for a Red Sox Triple-A club with 58 and counting.
There's just one problem...
While Ward seems like a slam-dunk option to fill White's role on the postseason roster, it is not as simple as just recalling him from Triple-A, as he's not on the 40-man roster. The Red Sox 40-man roster currently sits at 39; however, the impending returns of Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo mean the team will have to either designate two players for assignment or move someone to the 60-day IL.
Luckily, there are several candidates for the latter: in White, should he be unable to return for the postseason, designated hitter Masataka Yoshida, utility man Anthony Seigler and reliever Justin Slaten, all of whom appear unlikely to return prior to the end of the season.
Is Ward actually an option?
Interim manager Chad Tracy was asked about the possibility of Ward joining the big-league club during his weekly appearance on WEEI's 'Rich and Ken with Ted Johnson' Show on Wednesday afternoon. "I think that'd be considered for sure," he said when asked about the possibility of Ward joining the big-league team. "It's really hard to predict what a roster could look like, but you definitely can't ignore a 60-stolen-base player," he continued.
However, Tracy cautioned that a pinch runner is a last resort for a team when it's trailing, and teams must consider other options, like whether it would be more valuable to add another right-handed bat or a better defender to the roster. Though Ward does profile as an above-average outfield defender.
Up next for the Sox
After falling 4-2 in Tuesday night's series opener, the Red Sox will look to even up the three-game set with the Texas Rangers in game two of three from Globe Life Field on Wednesday night. Rookie left-hander Jake Bennett (9-7, 3.69 ERA) will get the start for Boston opposite fellow southpaw MacKenzie Gore (8-11, 4.62 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

After a historic July that saw the Boston Red Sox use high-leverage arms on a near-nightly basis, one of baseball's best bullpens became injury-ravaged, losing Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, and Justin Slaten to fatigue-related injuries. The losses of Whitlock, Slaten, and Guerrero forced interim manager Chad Tracy to turn to other relievers in high-leverage spots. Among those arms is right-hander Greg Weissert, who, after a brief trip to Triple-A Worcester, has come up huge for the bullpen.
In his first 48 appearances of the season, Weissert posted a 3.97 ERA in 45.1 innings pitched. The 31-year-old right-hander struggled in particular when taking over in situations with men already on base, allowing 13 of 29 inherited runners to score, which, at the time, was the third-most among all relievers.
After needing 34 pitches to get through an inning in Boston's 13-inning marathon win over the Chicago White Sox on Aug. 6, Weissert fell victim to the numbers game, getting optioned to Triple-A Worcester on Aug. 7 in favor of a fresher arm. However, it wound up being just a six-day trip as he was recalled on Aug. 13 when the team placed Whitlock on the IL.
In 12 appearances since being recalled, Weissert has more than made up for the losses of Whitlock, who returned on Aug. 29, Guerrero, who is slated to return ahead of Wednesday's game in Texas and Slaten. He's allowed only two earned runs on 11 hits, striking out 13 and walking only four in 10.2 innings of work. Most importantly, Weissert has performed much better when entering 'dirty' innings, allowing only one of seven inherited runners to score.
Despite Whitlock's return and Guerrero's imminent return, Weissert's reemergence as a reliable option will help in the final 11 games of the regular season and the postseason run, as Tracy announced Tuesday that Slaten will not return in 2026 after undergoing a PRP injection in his right elbow to treat degenerative changes in his flexor mass.

item.content:encoded:
Jake Bennett might not be Garrett Crochet, but the 25-year-old rookie has done an admirable job this season filling in for the injured Boston Red Sox ace. In fact, the youngster looked pretty Crochet-like with a 2.64 ERA in the first half, despite relying much less on the strikeout to generate that success.
However, as we race toward October, it's time to start thinking about the postseason rotation, and we could see Bennett as the odd man out. Since August 1, the youngster has made seven starts and posted a 5.26 ERA.
The way he's performed over his last three starts has been interesting. On August 29, he twirled six scoreless innings against the New York Yankees while allowing just three hits. On September 3, he took the ball against the Baltimore Orioles and again went six deep, this time surrendering three runs. The two outings were basically the opposite ends of the spectrum of what we'd consider acceptable for a starter in the playoff rotation.
That Orioles start had a hidden concern, though. Bennett served up two homers, and it would prove prophetic for the next time he took the mound. That came on September 9 against the hapless Los Angeles Angels, who torched him for six earned runs over 5 1/3 innings. Bennett got taken deep three times in the affair and allowed eight balls to be hit over 100 miles per hour. His average exit velo for the start was a whopping 95.6 miles per hour.
At the same time, his chief competition for a spot in the playoff rotation, Ranger Suarez, might be rounding into form. The veteran struggled mightily in August after returning from the groin issue that landed him on the IL back in July, posting a 5.70 ERA for the month.
His lone start of September, though, was vintage Suarez, turning in seven shutout innings while allowing just five hits and a walk and generating a whole lot of soft contact.
If Ranger Suarez can prove he's back, he'll swipe Jake Bennett's spot in the Red Sox's playoff rotation
One start doesn't erase all the concern, but Suarez earned the second All-Star nod of his career thanks to his mostly stellar work in the first half. It's not unreasonable to assume that his string of uninspiring August performances was simply due to him knocking off the rust after being on the IL.
For Bennett, there's an added layer. With 105 innings already on his ledger in the majors and another 39 1/3 frames for the WooSox, he's well past what he's used to. In his first minor league season back in 2023, he pitched 63 frames. He missed the entire 2024 season after undergoing Tommy John surgery, and then came back to throw 75 1/3 innings last season.
Essentially, his 144 1/3 combined innings this year alone are greater than the 138 1/3 inning workload he's carried the last three years combined. He can say that the increased run hasn't affected him, but if the results on the field tell a different story, then that's the likely case.
There are two other factors to consider in the event of a proverbial tie. One, the Red Sox gave Suarez $130 million over the winter for a reason. Contracts shouldn't give an underperforming player a boost over a younger, cheaper option, but if all else is equal, it can help to be the deciding factor.
More importantly, Suarez is experienced in October. During his time with the Phillies, he's thrown 42 2/3 playoff innings and owns a 1.48 postseason ERA. That experience, and more importantly, excellence, matters, especially when it seems that the other option is running out of gas.

item.content:encoded:
One miserable inning was enough to put the Red Sox in a hole. A pair of missed opportunities prevented them from climbing out of it.
Patrick Sandoval endured a brutal 44-pitch second inning in which the Rangers scored four times, and the Red Sox repeatedly came up empty with runners on base in a 4-2 loss Tuesday night at Globe Life Field.
Boston (82-69) opened its final road trip of the regular season with a loss and fell to 7-6 in September. The Red Sox did, however, move another step closer to securing a postseason berth after Toronto was routed by Detroit, reducing Boston’s magic number to five.
Any potential celebration will have to wait until after the Red Sox leave Texas. Even if Boston wins the final two games of the series, Toronto is off Thursday and would remain mathematically alive entering Friday.
Sandoval’s night began when he struck out the first four Rangers he faced before everything unraveled in a second inning that seemed as though it might never end.
With two outs, Brandon Nimmo and Ezequiel Duran delivered hard-hit singles at 106.3 mph and 105.3 mph, respectively. Elias Díaz followed by pulling a two-run double into left field to give Texas a 2-0 lead.
Sandoval never recovered walking former Sox catcher Danny Jansen and Justin Foscue before Corey Seager dropped a bloop single into shallow left, just beyond the reach of Trevor Story, allowing two more runs to score. By the time Sandoval finally escaped, he had thrown 44 pitches in the inning and Boston trailed 4-0.
Sandoval lasted just 2 2/3 innings and saw his ERA climb to 4.99.
“They drug at bats out on him,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters postgame. “It looked like he was going to get out of there with Diaz, that was a long at bat, I think one of those pitches was close and then he hits the double in the corner and it was just a struggle, we just couldn’t get out of the inning.”
The left-hander’s return from injury provided Boston with some needed innings after he was activated July 9, and he delivered several quality outings along the way. But with the postseason approaching, his place on the October roster has become increasingly uncertain.
Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle and Jake Bennett are ahead of him in the rotation picture, while Brayan Bello has found success in a bulk role. Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck are also attempting to return before the postseason.
Patrick Sandoval strikes out the side in the 1st.
Justin Foscue made him throw 9 pitches to start the game. Needed 19 total to finish the inning. pic.twitter.com/qpUpDLA5Rc
Sandoval will have time to try and clean things up, but it’s looking as if the Red Sox are better suited with the lefty as a spectator when they inevitably travel to the Bronx.
Boston’s offense quickly cut the deficit in half against Jacob deGrom.
Nick Sogard jumped on a pitch in the third and sent it down the right-field line for a two-run homer, pulling the Red Sox within 4-2.
Sogard didn’t hit his first major league homer until his 322nd plate appearance Aug. 19. He has now hit five in his last 99 plate appearances, all coming over a 24-game span.
The versatile infielder contributed in other ways, too. Sogard perfectly executed a sacrifice bunt in the fifth to move two runners into scoring position and later made an athletic play to complete a 1-4-3 double play.
But the Red Sox couldn’t capitalize on their opportunities against deGrom. The Texas right-hander held Boston to three hits and struck out eight over five innings while maintaining a fastball around 97 mph.

ARLINGTON, Texas — MacKenzie Gore starts Wednesday night for the Texas Rangers against the Boston Red Sox, who have rookie left-hander Jake Bennett scheduled. First pitch at Globe Life Field is 7:05 p.m. CT on Rangers Sports Network.
Gore’s 31 starts are the most in the majors. In his first season with Texas, he is 8-11 with a 4.62 ERA and has struck out 172 batters over 161 2/3 innings. He was an All-Star with the Washington Nationals in 2025.
Saturday, Texas activated Nathan Eovaldi from the injured list and moved him to the bullpen. That left Gore, Jacob deGrom, Kumar Rocker, and Cal Quantrill as the Rangers’ starters.
MacKenzie Gore’s Last Start In Phoenix
Gore last pitched Friday at Chase Field. The Arizona Diamondbacks scored 4 runs on 4 doubles against him in the fifth inning, and he was charged with 4 runs on 5 hits in 4-plus innings. He walked 3 and struck out 2. Arizona won 9-1, and Texas went 1-for-8 with runners in scoring position.
One night earlier, the Rangers lost 4-3 in Seattle after leading 3-0. Rangers manager Skip Schumaker put the two losses together after Friday’s game.
“You’ve got to flush it quickly and try to go about it in a different way tomorrow,” Schumaker said. “Brutal couple of days. There’s no sugarcoating it. But we have a chance to flush it tonight and to win tomorrow.”
Texas won the next two games, 6-2 on Saturday and 7-6 on Sunday.
On Aug. 26 at Rate Field, the Chicago White Sox scored 4 runs on 8 hits against Gore in 3 2/3 innings. He walked 4 in the 10-4 loss. Before that start, Texas had won nine straight games Gore started. He was 2-1 with a 3.32 ERA over his previous eight outings dating to July 12.
deGrom had allowed 8 runs in Chicago the night before, tying a career high, and neither starter finished four innings.
“It starts with starting pitching,” Schumaker explained that night. “I’ve said since day one that the health and production of our starting pitching was going to carry us. We acquired Gore and we knew we had deGrom and [Eovaldi]. We felt pretty good about it. These last two starts were not what they wanted; not what we were thinking was going to happen after winning the first game here.”
“That’s not what we thought we’re going to get,” Schumaker continued. “I don’t think they would tell you [they expected] that either.”
Jake Bennett’s Rookie Season With The Red Sox
Bennett, 25, is 9-7 with a 3.69 ERA. The 6-foot-6 left-hander was a second-round pick of the Nationals in 2022 out of the University of Oklahoma. Boston acquired him from Washington in the offseason. Gore pitched for the Nationals from 2023 to 2025.
Last Wednesday against the Los Angeles Angels at Fenway Park, Bennett allowed 6 runs on 9 hits over 5 1/3 innings in a 6-4 loss.
Boston is 82-68 and third in the American League East. The Red Sox hold an American League wild-card spot with 12 games left. Texas is 74-76 and one game behind the Houston Astros in the American League West, and Houston holds the tiebreaker.
In Tuesday’s opener, deGrom faces Boston left-hander Patrick Sandoval. Right-hander Sonny Gray starts Thursday’s finale for the Red Sox, and Texas has not announced its starter for that game.

We've reached the "wake me up for the playoffs" portion of the Boston Red Sox season.
The Red Sox have 12 games remaining on their 2026 regular-season schedule. As of Monday, they sit comfortably in the second American League Wild Card spot with a six-game lead. They're 4.5 games behind the New York Yankees in the Wild Card standings, so barring a shocking development, they'll visit the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series for the second consecutive year.
Which 26 players will the Red Sox bring with them to the Bronx? Who's on the chopping block? Here's our 26-man playoff roster projection with 15 days until Game 1:
MORE RED SOX
Catcher (2): Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
Cuts: None
The Red Sox could theoretically cut Wong since he'd barely see the field with Rutschman healthy. If Rutschman went down in that scenario, Mickey Gasper could go behind the plate... but that wouldn't be pretty.
Here's the problem with that approach: If Rutschman gets hurt and the Red Sox add a replacement catcher mid-series, Rutschman would be ineligible for the next playoff round. So if he got hurt in the Wild Card Series, he'd be ineligible for the ALDS and eligible to return in the ALCS.
Putting Wong on the playoff roster ensures that if Rutschman goes down, they won't need to add a mid-series replacement with Wong and Gasper already on board. And while Wong isn't exactly Pudge Rodriguez defensively, he's better than Gasper behind the dish.
Infield (7): Willson Contreras, Trevor Story, Caleb Durbin, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, Andruw Monasterio
Cuts: Curtis Mead (IL), Anthony Seigler (IL)
Even with Wong on the roster, Gasper's incredible offensive upside shown in August earns him a roster spot as a bench bat. Monasterio is on the bubble, but recent injuries may have cleared his path to a bench role.
It doesn't look like Mead (wrist) will be healthy in time for the start of the postseason.
Outfield (5): Jarren Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
Cuts: Eli White (IL), Masataka Yoshida (IL), Nate Eaton
The big question mark here is White's health, as the speedster was recently placed on the 10-day injured list with a foot ligament injury. He'll play a key bench role if healthy, but if he isn't, Jones or Eaton are the top candidates for that fifth outfield spot. We're leaning Jones because of his ability to mash left-handers.
Yoshida (hamstring) probably isn't coming back this year.
Starting rotation (3): Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suarez
Cuts: Patrick Sandoval
Sandoval just hasn't been reliable, so he draws the short straw. Jake Bennett and the returning Garrett Crochet move to the bullpen -- assuming Crochet is healthy enough to give one or two quality innings in relief.
Bullpen (9): Garrett Crochet, Jake Bennett, Brayan Bello, Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, Erik Miller, Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock, Aroldis Chapman
Cuts: Justin Slaten (IL), Tanner Houck (IL), Johan Oviedo (IL), Alec Gamboa, Jovani Moran, Raymond Burgos
If Slaten's elbow is healthy, he's in, but it doesn't currently look like it will be since he was recently shut down from throwing.
Crochet is trending toward being ready just in time for October. So is Houck, but he hasn't pitched in a big-league game since May 2025, and he hasn't looked sharp in his rehab outings. While his upside is intriguing, we'd leave him off the initial playoff roster.
Brayan Bello makes the cut as a bulk arm after excelling in that role throughout the second half.

item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras is back with the Red Sox, activated Sunday from the injured list for their finale against the Royals. He collected two hits and a walk in the 4-1 win.
The Red Sox didn’t need to think hard about how to open a spot on the active roster: infielder Anthony Seigler went on the injured list with a right wrist issue.
“We talked a lot about as guys were getting healthy, the conversation was like, ‘What are you going to do?’” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “Stuff’s going to happen, which it always does.”
Contreras missed a dozen games because of a left hamstring strain.
After playing through the leg problem for about a month, Contreras asked the front office to let him more thoroughly rest, figuring a September timeout would serve him well down the stretch and into the playoffs.
On his first day back, he tested it plenty — hustling to first base and advancing to second on an error, moving from first to third on a single.
“I ran a lot today on the field, and my hammy feels pretty good,” Contreras said. “I won’t lie: If I wasn’t feeling really good in [Double-A] Portland, I wasn’t going to play tonight.”
Tracy said: “The point of [going on the IL] was to get [the hamstring] to a point where he felt confident in it, where he can go out and play and not have to worry. And at least like to think we’ve got to that point, which is good.”
In a two-game tuneup with Double-A Portland, Contreras went 2 for 7 with three strikeouts and no walks.
His appearance Saturday yielded a strange episode in the fourth inning. After a ball moved the count to 1-and-1, he called timeout, seemingly to get pine tar. Plate umpire Daniel Bytheway called him back to the plate.
Contreras then all but stopped participating in the plate appearance, leaving the bat on his shoulders for the next four pitches. He struck out looking.
On his way back to the dugout, drawing boos from the Portland crowd, Contreras tossed his bat back toward the plate.
“I didn’t even know until somebody showed it to me this [Sunday] morning,” Tracy said before the game. “I haven’t even seen him and asked him that yet. I think that’s something to do with pine tar.”
Contreras said later Sunday: “I don’t know. You can go ask the umpire. His name is Gary. Thank you.”
The Red Sox didn’t have a diagnosis on Seigler, who hurt himself on a seemingly random swing Saturday, but intended to send him for tests in the coming days.
As the rotation turns
The Red Sox will keep their starting pitchers in line against the Rangers: Patrick Sandoval on Tuesday, Jake Bennett on Wednesday, Sonny Gray on Thursday. Brayan Bello is bumped back to the bullpen following a one-start cameo.
Rehab roundup
The Red Sox will bring Tyron Guerrero (right shoulder inflammation) to Texas and activate him during the Rangers series. They haven’t decided which day. He is eligible to return Wednesday.
Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) told NESN he is planning to return for the Rays series next weekend.
“We’ll call that a goal. It’s not a guarantee,” Tracy said. “It really is dependent on strength numbers in the quad and making sure that’s appropriate, and then he gets through all the sprint volume stuff first, and then we’ll see where he’s at.”
The Sox will leave it up to Rafaela, Tracy added, whether he wants to go on a rehab assignment before returning. Triple-A Worcester is the last affiliate still in season.
Justin Slaten (right elbow inflammation) still has not resumed throwing.
Guest of honor
Beverly native Beckett Connolly, a 10-year-old liver cancer survivor and transplant recipient, threw out a ceremonial first pitch — to hefty applause from the Fenway Park crowd.
